motion: This house would adopt a four-day working week
text: Of the 61 companies in Britain's four-day week pilot, 56 kept the four-day week going after the trial ended.
label: supported
reason: The official pilot report (Autonomy, Feb 2023) says 56 of the 61 companies are continuing, 18 permanently.

motion: This house would adopt a four-day working week
text: Revenue at the firms in the UK four-day week pilot barely moved during the trial, it only went up about 1.4 percent.
label: supported
reason: The pilot report says revenue stayed broadly the same over the trial period, rising by 1.4% on average.

motion: This house would adopt a four-day working week
text: Iceland's shorter working week trials covered about a fifth of the country's entire workforce.
label: contradicted
reason: The trials involved just over 2,500 workers, a little more than 1% of Iceland's working population, not a fifth.

motion: This house would adopt a four-day working week
text: Firms in the UK pilot reported revenue up 35 percent on previous years while they were on a four-day week.
label: missing_context
reason: The 35% is a comparison with the same period in earlier years from respondent firms; over the trial itself revenue was broadly flat (up 1.4%), so it says nothing about the four-day week's effect.

motion: This house would adopt a four-day working week
text: Half the firms that turned down a place in the UK pilot did so because their customers wouldn't accept a four-day week.
label: unverifiable
reason: No public source records why firms declined to join the pilot.

motion: This house would ban smartphones in UK schools
text: A study of 30 English secondary schools found pupils at schools that restrict phones had no better mental wellbeing than pupils at schools that don't.
label: supported
reason: Goodyear et al. 2025 (SMART Schools, Lancet Regional Health Europe) found no evidence of a difference in wellbeing between restrictive and permissive schools.

motion: This house would ban smartphones in UK schools
text: Barely half of children in Britain have their own mobile phone by the age of eleven.
label: contradicted
reason: Ofcom's 2025 children's media use report says nine in ten (91%) children own their own mobile phone by age 11.

motion: This house would ban smartphones in UK schools
text: Fewer than half of secondary schools in England stop pupils using their phones during the school day.
label: contradicted
reason: The Children's Commissioner's survey of 19,000 schools found 90% of secondary schools (and 99.8% of primaries) already have such policies.

motion: This house would ban smartphones in UK schools
text: An LSE study found that banning phones in schools raised pupils' test scores by 6.4 percent.
label: missing_context
reason: Beland and Murphy (CEP DP1350) found a gain of 6.41% of a standard deviation, not 6.4% higher scores, concentrated in low achievers, from schools in four English cities.

motion: This house would ban smartphones in UK schools
text: Most secondary pupils who hand in a phone at school have a second phone hidden on them.
label: unverifiable
reason: No survey or official data measures how many pupils carry a second phone.

motion: This house would abolish the BBC licence fee
text: The BBC's own estimate is that more than 12 percent of households that need a TV licence are evading it.
label: supported
reason: The 2024/25 Licence Fee Trust Statement gives an estimated evasion rate of 12.52%.

motion: This house would abolish the BBC licence fee
text: A TV licence costs less than 150 pounds a year, that's under 40p a day.
label: contradicted
reason: DCMS set the fee at £180 from 1 April 2026 (about 49p a day); it was already £174.50 in 2025/26.

motion: This house would abolish the BBC licence fee
text: Licence fee income actually went up last year, by 5 percent to over 3.8 billion pounds, so the licence fee isn't in decline.
label: missing_context
reason: Income rose to £3,843m only because the fee rose from £159 to £169.50; paid-for licences fell by about 314,000 and estimated evasion rose.

motion: This house would abolish the BBC licence fee
text: 3.6 million households now say they don't need a TV licence, that's over 600 million pounds a year the BBC is losing.
label: missing_context
reason: The £617m is what the BBC could gain if those households chose to buy a licence; they declared they don't watch licensable content, so it isn't money owed or lost to evasion.

motion: This house would abolish the BBC licence fee
text: Most people who stopped paying the licence fee still watch BBC programmes every week through clips on YouTube and social media.
label: unverifiable
reason: No published data tracks the viewing of people who cancelled their licence.

motion: This house would make public transport free
text: Luxembourg became the first country in the world to make all its public transport free, back in 2020.
label: supported
reason: Luxembourg's Ministry of Mobility says that since 1 March 2020 it is the first country where buses, trains (except first class) and trams are free.

motion: This house would make public transport free
text: When Tallinn made public transport free, use went up 14 percent and car trips fell by 10 percent.
label: missing_context
reason: Cats et al. (Transportation, 2017) report both figures, but much of the shift came from walking (down 40%) and total car vehicle-km rose 31%, an increase in car traffic.

motion: This house would make public transport free
text: The two pound bus fare cap barely made a difference, it added only about a million extra bus journeys.
label: contradicted
reason: The government says the last £2 fare cap saw an estimated 30 million more bus journeys in its first 10 months.

motion: This house would make public transport free
text: Most of the bus routes cut in Britain over the last decade were cut because they were running nearly empty.
label: unverifiable
reason: Route withdrawals are counted, but no public source records the reasons for most of them.

motion: This house would make public transport free
text: Pensioners with free bus passes make most of their trips on buses that would be running half empty anyway.
label: unverifiable
reason: No published data links concessionary trips to bus occupancy.

motion: This house would ban cars from city centres
text: In 2024, 409 pedestrians were killed on Britain's roads.
label: supported
reason: DfT's pedestrian factsheet 2024 says 409 pedestrians were killed in Great Britain in 2024.

motion: This house would ban cars from city centres
text: Most pedestrians killed in Britain die on country roads, not in towns and cities.
label: contradicted
reason: DfT: in 2020 to 2024, 66% of pedestrian fatalities were on roads in urban areas and 29% in rural areas.
key: 66% of pedestrian fatalities occurred on roads in urban areas

motion: This house would ban cars from city centres
text: Pedestrian deaths on Britain's roads went up again in 2024.
label: missing_context
reason: Deaths rose only 1% while distance walked rose 2%, so the risk per mile fell, and deaths are down 39% since 2004.

motion: This house would ban cars from city centres
text: Air pollution kills around a hundred thousand people in the UK every year.
label: contradicted
reason: UKHSA guidance puts the annual mortality of human-made air pollution at roughly the equivalent of 28,000 to 36,000 deaths.

motion: This house would ban cars from city centres
text: Most people who drive into British city centres for work live somewhere with no direct bus route.
label: unverifiable
reason: No national data links city-centre commuters' homes to bus route coverage.
